title: Office Design

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Throughout San Francisco and Silicon Valley, cash-rich technology firms have built or are erecting bold, futuristic headquarters that convey their brands to employees and customers. For example, RideGo is a transport network company that is hoping to recast its reputation for secrecy and rugged competitiveness by designing an entirely see-through head office. It is expected to have some interior areas, as well as a park, that will be open to the public. The exteriors of the new buildings will attract most attention, but it is their interiors that should be watched more closely. The big idea championed by the technology industry is the concept of working in various spaces around an office rather than at a fixed workstation. There are 'libraries' where employees can work quietly, as well as coffee shops, cafés and outdoor spaces all on the premises for meetings and phone calls. Workers may still have an assigned desk but they are not expected to be there, and they routinely go to different parts of the office to do various tasks. Other industries have experimented with 'activity-based working', but tech is ahead.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A fluid working environment is meant to allow for more chance encounters, which could spur new ideas and spark unexpected collaborations. Smaller tech start-up companies such as LikeMe embrace open-plan offices. They are designed to encourage employees to bump into one another in common spaces and in their central office they have a rooftop garden dedicated to this purpose. Communal areas are meant to be casual and alluring, and sometimes they are made into living-room-like spaces. For offices to feel like home, it helps to hire a designer with expertise in residential real-estate, says Elizabeth Greenway of LikeMe. In common areas at the firm's offices, there are TVs, couches and bookshelves, and framed photos of a few employees add to the effect.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: For those who laugh at the creative benefits of being surrounded by pictures of colleagues, there are more tangible payoffs. The lack of fixed workstations shrinks the amount of expensive real estate given to employees without leaving them feeling too squeezed. Tech firms devote around 14 square metres to each employee, around a quarter less than other industries, according to Randy Howder at Gensler, a design firm. Young workers are thought to be more productive in these varied environments, which are reminiscent of the way people study when they attend university. One drawback, however, is that locating colleagues can be a problem. Employees need to track each other down through text messages and messaging apps. Collaborative spaces can also expose generational tensions, says Louise Mozingo, an architecture professor at the University of California, Berkeley. Tech firms' older employees can struggle to adjust to moving around during the day and dislike the frequent disruptions that come from large, open-plan offices. For example, many of PeopleForce's employees do not like their office because of the noise, and others also resent the massive distances they will need to walk. It seems that these problems could be minimised if the employees' needs were taken into account by the designers.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Tech firms are increasingly keen to use their own products in their headquarters. James Hong, the chief executive of Vitan, a chipmaking firm whose graphics processing units are widely used in artificial-intelligence programs, says his firm pians to introduce facial recognition for entry into its new headquarters, due to open later this year. Vitan will also install cameras to recognise what food people are taking from the cafeteria and charge them accordingly, eliminating the need for a queue and cashier. A self-driving shuttle will eventually zip between its various buildings. And Vitan's own artificial intelligence will monitor when employees arrive and leave, with the ostensible aim of adjusting the building's heating and cooling systems.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A less controversial trend is for unusual office interiors. These can distinguish companies in the minds of their employees, act as a recruiting tool and also give staff a reason to come into the office rather than work from home. The top two floors of PeopleForce Tower, for example, will be used not as corner offices for executives but as an airy lounge for employees, where they can work and gaze out at the views over a coffee. And for companies that do not ship a physical product, such offices can serve as important daily reminders of culture and purpose. Hometel is a tech firm that enables people to rent out their homes. Instead of offering generic meeting rooms with generic names, Hometel designed each of its meeting spaces after one of its rental listings, such as a Bedouin tent from Morocco.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Such workspaces remind staff that they are choosing not just an employer but a way of life. Now the emphasis is increasingly on amenities that help employees save time. Larger firms offer their staff something akin to the services used by the extremely wealthy, helping employees to find homes, adopt pets and the like. Some large tech groups offer on-site health care. The effect of all this is that the typical office at a technology firm such as RideGo is becoming a prosperous, self-contained village. Employees have fewer reasons than ever to go off site. Other industries would be wise to take time to watch how tech firms are structuring their work environments.
